name: the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens
title: Ancient Trees in the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, Hobart: 6 to Find
meta_description: Six remarkable trees at 42 degrees south, five of them from other continents and the sixth Australian without being Tasmanian.
intro: Five of the six trees mapped here came from somewhere else, and the sixth is Australian without being Tasmanian. A Douglas fir out of the Pacific Northwest went into the ground in 1894, seven years before the Australian colonies federated, and measured 30 metres when the National Trust looked at it in 2014. Two giant sequoias planted together in 1879 still mark the entrance drive. A Queensland kauri, a rainforest tree from the warm wet coast far to the north, reaches 39 metres here at 42 degrees south and is listed on Hobart's register under four headings at once, where most trees carry one. A chir pine from the dry Himalayan foothills droops needles thirty centimetres long. The spotted gum is the local one, and even it grows wild in New South Wales rather than on this island.
